main_damage_causes: Near-total omission of Ariana's backstory (the attack, the magic turning inward, the rages, the sweetness, the family's sacrifice) removes her as a character and reduces her to an abstraction, gutting the moral and emotional foundation of Dumbledore's arc
Erasure of Aberforth's specific bond with Ariana destroys the relationship that gives his grief and resentment its emotional specificity and tragic weight

Omission of the three-way duel and the ambiguity of who killed Ariana removes the most devastating dimension of Dumbledore's guilt — the possibility that he directly caused her death — softening the 'greater good' theme from potential self-implication to mere negligence

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Sitting Room) - Aberforth's account of Ariana reduced to a single line
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book provides an extensive, emotionally devastating account of Ariana's backstory: her attack by Muggle boys at age six, the magic turning inward and driving her mad, her father's imprisonment, the family's forced secrecy, her rages and moments of sweetness, her special bond with Aberforth (feeding goats, calming her down), Albus's neglect of her in favour of Grindelwald, and the three-way duel in which she died. This is a multi-scene, deeply characterised portrayal of a traumatised girl whose life and death anchor the entire moral weight of Dumbledore's arc.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Aberforth's entire account of Ariana is collapsed into a single line: 'My brother sacrificed many things, Mr. Potter, in his journey to find power, including her. She was devoted to him — he gave her everything, but time.' No attack, no magic turning inward, no illness, no rages, no sweetness, no father's sacrifice, no goats, no special bond with Aberforth, no three-way duel, no ambiguity about who killed her.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Ariana's full backstory is the structural foundation of Dumbledore's greatest flaw and the saga's central moral theme ('the greater good'). The book spends pages establishing her as a specific, vivid, tragically human figure — not a symbol but a person with a particular relationship to each brother. The film reduces her entirely to a rhetorical abstraction in Aberforth's argument against Albus. The audience never learns what happened to her, what she suffered, what she was like, or what the cost of her death actually was. This is not a trimming; it is the removal of the entire foundation that makes Dumbledore's arc meaningful.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Sitting Room) - Aberforth's relationship with Ariana erased
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Aberforth explicitly states he was Ariana's favourite, not Albus. He could get her to eat when she refused their mother, calm her during rages, and she helped him feed the goats. This bond is the emotional core of his grief and his fury at Albus — he was her primary caregiver and lost her personally, not just as a family member.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film contains no mention of Aberforth's special bond with Ariana. His grief is present (he keeps her portrait, says 'she'll always be beautiful') but its specific source — that he was her protector and closest companion — is entirely absent. His resentment of Albus is framed only in terms of power and neglect, not in terms of this intimate lost relationship.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Without the established bond, Aberforth's grief and his portrait-keeping read as generic brotherly loss rather than the loss of someone he personally sustained and loved above all others. The emotional specificity that makes Aberforth a tragic figure in his own right — not just a foil for Albus — is gone.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Sitting Room) - The three-way duel and ambiguity of Ariana's death omitted
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Aberforth recounts that he confronted Albus and Grindelwald, Grindelwald used the Cruciatus Curse on him, all three began dueling, and Ariana — trying to help — was caught in the crossfire. No one knows which of the three killed her. This ambiguity is morally essential: it means Albus may have killed his own sister, and can never know.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film provides no account of how Ariana died. There is no duel, no Cruciatus, no ambiguity. The audience is only told she was 'sacrificed' by Albus's ambition — implying passive neglect rather than a possible direct act. The specific horror of not knowing who cast the fatal spell is completely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The ambiguity of Ariana's death is what makes Dumbledore's guilt so devastating and so irreducible — he can never know if he killed her. The film's vague framing of her death as 'sacrifice' softens this into a manageable moral failing rather than a potentially unforgivable one. This directly damages the depth of Dumbledore's character and the seriousness of the 'greater good' theme.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Bathilda's house) - Ariana's photograph described only as 'a curiously compelling young girl'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book describes Ariana's portrait as showing a girl with 'a kind of a vacant sweetness' — a specific characterisation that encodes her condition (the blankness of trauma, the residual gentleness beneath it). It is a precise, loaded image.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film script describes the photograph of Ariana as showing 'a curiously compelling young girl' — an aestheticising description that frames her in terms of mysterious beauty rather than the vacant sweetness of a damaged child. Hermione later in Scene 3 calls her 'beautiful.'
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's 'vacant sweetness' signals Ariana's psychological state and the tragedy of what was done to her. The film's 'curiously compelling' and 'beautiful' reframe her as an aesthetically interesting figure, removing the note of damage and loss. This is a small but telling shift that shapes how the audience will receive all subsequent references to her.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (King's Cross) - Dumbledore's desire to see Ariana used only as a negative illustration
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the books, Dumbledore's longing to use the Resurrection Stone to see Ariana again is part of a complex portrait of unresolved grief and guilt. His desire to speak to her is understandable and pitiable even as it is shown to be dangerous. Ariana functions here as the object of his deepest, most private sorrow.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's King's Cross scene has Harry ask 'You wanted to see Ariana again, didn't you, sir?' and Dumbledore confirm simply 'Yes.' This is faithful in outline, but because the audience has received no backstory about Ariana — no account of who she was, what happened to her, what she meant to Albus — the moment lands as an abstract acknowledgment rather than an emotionally resonant confession. Ariana is a name, not a person the audience has been made to know.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The emotional payoff of this King's Cross moment depends entirely on the audience having been given Ariana's story. Without it, Dumbledore's admission is stripped of weight. The film has the callback without having done the work to make it land. This is a downstream consequence of the earlier omissions, but it represents a distinct moment where Ariana's function in Dumbledore's arc fails on screen.
